newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hyundai Motor's Vietnam plans hit snag.
newsitem.headline: Hyundai Motor's Vietnam plans hit snag.

text.p: Vietnamese Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet is not in favour of granting a licence for a proposed joint venture between South Korea's Hyundai Motor Co and the government, Vice-Minister for Industry Nguyen Xuan Chuan said on Monday.
"I know that the prime minister is not in favour of the Hyundai project, he wants to decline it," Chuan told Reuters. "He's saying that 14 licences is too many now."
Chuan said government ministries were trying to persuade Kiet to approve the project, which would take the number of licences issued for foreign car makers in Vietnam to 15.
Officials at Hyundai's Vietnam offices were not immediately available for comment.
A senior Ministry of Planning and Investment official had said last month that approval for the roughly $250-million project with the Interior Ministry would be granted before the end of 1996.

Some vehicle makers have complained that too many licences have been approved for a market which stood at just 39,800 units in 1995. However, Chuan has argued that there is no need to limit the number of foreign joint ventures.
He told a recent car industry conference that all-vehicle demand would more than double to 80,800 units by 2005.
However, he said that if demand continued to outstrip projections at its current rate, the annual market could stand at 105,000 units by 2005, equivalent to 77 percent of production capacity.

Six of the licensed ventures, which have a combined car output capacity of some 30,000 a year, have already started production. However, their output is limited by a government quota -- 6,000 cars in 1996 -- on imports of unassembled vehicles, known as complete knockdown kits (CKDs).
Chuan, rejecting the theory that too many licences had been issued, pointed to the government's policy of obliging car makers to produce a rising share of their components locally.
"For anybody who is willing to meet this requirement, we should give a licence," he said.
